prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene.

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, credited to MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. It is a prediction (the 2011 continuum model with flat bands at a specific twist angle) followed seven years later by an unambiguous discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, reproduced by many independent groups and extended to other moire systems. Nobody in round 1 disputed that the result is real. The chair's own summary records that B017 has the broadest opening support (top three on five ballots), and I note that only as a pointer to where members' scientific judgement overlaps, not as evidence. The citation I now propose names only the prediction and the observation of the phases, not the pairing mechanism and not the wider twistronics field, which several colleagues on both sides asked for and which I accept. That wording answers the chair's maturity question, because the discovery is secure whatever the mechanism turns out to be.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is the weakest part of my position, and the round-1 exchange did not repair it. Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, the Dean, Young, Kim and Yazdani groups, and earlier twisted-bilayer band theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) all fall outside three names, and a three-person cap cannot be stretched to cover them. Bistritzer is the contested third seat, since Eriksson-Olle and Mehlig-Bernhard would accept two names. The mechanism of superconductivity is also still debated, and the 2010 graphene and 2016 topological-phase prizes mean that the area has been honoured before. B015 has the cleaner credit and the stronger maturity record, and I cannot honestly claim that B017 is better on those two axes.

responses.point: Kroll, Pearce-Mark and Olsson-Eva argue that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes because the magic-wavelength condition lets many atoms be interrogated at once with the lattice shift cancelled.
responses.response: That argument moves me. In round 1 I treated the clock as an increment on a recognised line, and the magic-wavelength condition is not supplied by either earlier prize, so it is a separate idea with its own figure of merit. I withdraw the overlap objection as a reason to rank B015 low, which is why B015 stays my first alternative and is now a real fallback rather than a polite one. What remains between us is the criterion. If the committee wants a measurement capability whose credit is clean, B015 wins. If it wants a discovery that opened a regime of physics, B017 does. I think the second criterion is closer to the spirit of the prize, but I do not claim it is decisive.

responses.point: Lindroth-Eva says the clock is not narrow, since it reaches fundamental-constant tests, geodesy and the definition of the second, and that B017 has the harder attribution problem; she asks whether my low ranking was a judgement about breadth or only a different weighting of discovery over invention.
responses.response: It is mostly the second. I accept that the clock's reach is real and already concrete, and I will not call it narrow. My point is about what kind of new knowledge the prize recognises. Her attribution point is fair and I have conceded it in my case against: B015 is cleaner than B017. But I disagree that the experimental credit in B017 is unsettled in a way that defeats the prize. The 2018 papers came from Jarillo-Herrero's group, the prediction is a single two-author paper, and a citation limited to those two things stays defensible even though Cao and others are left out.

responses.point: Johansson-Goran supports the same three names but is less relaxed about maturity because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, and wants the citation to make no claim about origin.
responses.response: I agree with the citation discipline and have rewritten my citation along those lines, so it no longer says anything about moire quantum matter as a field. On maturity we still differ in degree. A discovery prize is about whether the phenomenon is robust, and correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted graphene have been reproduced by several groups over eight years. The same test applied to the pulsar-timing background (B004), which I raised in round 1, would be harder to pass, so I would not defer B017 on this ground and keep B004 on the shortlist at the same time.

responses.point: Eriksson-Olle would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero for B017, and for B051 would keep Mele rather than Hasan in the third seat beside Kane and Molenkamp because the 2D and 3D discoveries differ in kind.
responses.response: On B051 his argument persuades me that a focused quantum spin Hall citation with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is cleaner than my Hasan variant, and I no longer press the Hasan configuration. On B017 I still keep Bistritzer. The 2011 prediction is a joint paper in which he is the first author, and a prize for that prediction that omits him would be hard to defend. I would accept two names only if the committee decides the citation should rest on the experiment plus MacDonald, and I regard that as second best.

uncertainties: Whether three names or two is the right credit for B017, and whether any wording can make the omission of Yuan Cao and the other experimental groups defensible.
Whether the committee will defer B017 on the unresolved superconducting mechanism despite the reproduced observations.
Whether a discovery that opened a new regime should outrank a clean, mature and reproduced invention such as B015, which is a question of criterion on which I may be weighting my own taste.
I am recalling priority details of the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper and of the 2018 experiments from memory and have not verified them independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my work is in string theory, gravitation and cosmology, and I have no documented connection to any shortlisted candidate, credited person or their institutions. As Secretary I note that field distance from condensed matter and metrology is a limit on my judgement, not a reason to recuse.
